    Natural-speech TRF on a real cohort¶

    An end-to-end walkthrough of TRFlearn on 17 participants listening to an audiobook, from the preprocessed recordings to threshold-free cluster-corrected group inference.

    This is the repository's one example built on a public, real EEG dataset rather than a simulation, and it is organised in two parts:

    • Part I — the envelope TRF. A single predictor, fitted the way the library is meant to be used, producing the classic auditory response. Everything the library offers around a fit — metric choice, design diagnostics, the whole plotting API, cohort statistics, bootstrap, TFCE — is exercised here.
    • Part II — adding phonemes and words. Two predictors from the audiobook's forced-aligned transcript enter the same model: the onset of every phoneme and of every word. This is where joint estimation, between-block collinearity, model comparison and the split of the explained variance between predictors become meaningful — and where the tidy envelope kernel stops being tidy, for reasons worth understanding. A last model codes every phoneme by its identity, one column each, as the original study did.
    Data Natural Speech (Di Liberto et al. 2015; Broderick et al. 2018), 17 subjects × 20 runs
    Recording BioSemi 128-channel ActiveTwo, 128 Hz, mastoid-referenced, ICA-cleaned
    Predictors acoustic envelope, plus phoneme and word onsets in Part II
    Window −150 to 450 ms, fitted with a 50 ms margin that is trimmed afterwards
    Fit cv="pooled", 5 block-stratified folds, ridge, λ chosen on R² and shared by the cohort (leave-one-subject-out)
    Inference TFCE, 1024 permutations, full channel × delay adjacency

    1 · The data¶

    The task. Healthy adult participants listened to a professionally recorded audiobook of Hemingway's The Old Man and the Sea, presented as 20 continuous runs of roughly three minutes each — about an hour of speech per person. There is no trial structure and nothing to respond to: subjects simply listened to uninterrupted natural narration while 128-channel EEG was recorded with a BioSemi ActiveTwo system at 512 Hz. That continuity is the point. Because the stimulus never stops, responses to successive acoustic events overlap continuously, and averaging cannot separate them — which is precisely the situation a temporal response function exists to handle.

    The recordings come from Di Liberto, O'Sullivan & Lalor (2015) and were extended by Broderick et al. (2018).

    Two public releases, and why both are needed. The same experiment was published twice, and neither release is self-sufficient:

    Field OpenNeuro (ds004408) Dryad (10.5061/dryad.070jc)
    State raw, unfiltered, unreferenced, 512 Hz the same signal at 128 Hz, still unreferenced
    Format BIDS / BrainVision, 128 scalp channels MATLAB .mat: eegData, mastoids, fs
    Mastoid channels absent present — the only way to re-reference
    Bad-channel flags present (*_channels.tsv) absent
    Stimuli .wav + forced-aligned .TextGrid precomputed 128 Hz envelopes

    OpenNeuro records which electrodes were bad; only Dryad carries the mastoids the original analysis referenced to. Reproducing the published pipeline needs both — which first requires knowing which OpenNeuro subject is which Dryad subject, since the two releases number their participants differently and neither provides a key.

    Recovering the correspondence. Correlating subjects directly does not work: everyone heard the same audiobook, so every pair shares the same stimulus-driven response and correlates at r ≈ 0.6 whether matched or not. The mapping was instead established by resampling OpenNeuro to 128 Hz, searching the lag between the two recordings of each run (OpenNeuro keeps a variable pre-roll of up to ~12 s; Dryad is trimmed to the audio), and requiring the same partner to win in every one of the 20 runs. At the correct lag a true pair reaches r ≈ 0.92–1.00 and wins consistently, while a subject with no counterpart changes partner run to run and never exceeds ~0.82. 18 of 19 subjects map one-to-one; OpenNeuro sub-003 and Dryad Subject5 have no partner and are dropped. A third, sub11, was excluded on inspection of its recordings. That is why this cohort has 17 members and no sub03 or sub11, and why subject numbering follows OpenNeuro's.

    Preprocessing already applied to the files read below.

    1. Re-referenced to the average of the two mastoids, and cropped to the length of the corresponding stimulus envelope.
    2. Montage biosemi128; channels flagged bad in OpenNeuro's channels.tsv are interpolated with spherical splines, so info['bads'] is empty in the saved files.
    3. ICA: extended Infomax, 20 components, fitted on the concatenated runs band-passed 1–40 Hz for the fit only. Artefact components were selected by hand from topography and spectrum.
    4. Applied per run. ica.apply is a fixed spatial projection, so the saved .fif files remain broadband — no temporal filter has touched them.

    The band-pass is therefore left to the analysis, and this notebook applies it explicitly: a linear-phase FIR, applied with its delay compensated so it is zero-phase. It is MNE's windowed design (firwin, Hamming window, 845 taps, 6.6 s) with a passband of 1.5–14 Hz and transitions of 0.5 and 1 Hz: −6 dB at 1.25 and 14.5 Hz, and more than 50 dB down from 1 Hz and from 15 Hz on. Those are the edges of the original study's filter, a Chebyshev type II IIR (order 4, 20 dB stopband) run forward and backward, whose nominal "1–15 Hz" are where its stopband begins: a FIR asked for 1–15 Hz would instead pass both edges whole, and with them the slow drifts below 1.5 Hz. A causal filter would shift every peak and corrupt exactly the latencies of interest; the FIR's phase is linear by construction rather than cancelled by a second pass, and its stopband is deeper. Like any zero-phase filter it is non-causal: it spreads every deflection to both sides in time, so a response can leak into the negative delays of a kernel.

    The predictors. The acoustic envelope is the magnitude of the Hilbert analytic signal of the waveform, resampled to the EEG's 128 Hz — a single continuous channel tracking how the speech's amplitude rises and falls. Part II adds two more from the forced-aligned .TextGrid files of the OpenNeuro release: a unit impulse at the onset of every phoneme, and one at the onset of every word. The transcript's clock starts with the audio, as the envelope's does; section 3 checks it.

    Getting the data. The preprocessed set is ~4 GB and lives outside this repository; the two source releases are ~22 GB together. Download them from the links above and apply the four steps described in the previous section, or point DATA_ROOT below at an existing copy.

    References¶

    Data

    • Di Liberto, G. M., O'Sullivan, J. A., & Lalor, E. C. (2015). Low-frequency cortical entrainment to speech reflects phoneme-level processing. Current Biology, 25(19), 2457–2465.
    • Broderick, M. P., Anderson, A. J., Di Liberto, G. M., Crosse, M. J., & Lalor, E. C. (2018). Electrophysiological correlates of semantic dissimilarity reflect the comprehension of natural, narrative speech. Current Biology, 28(5), 803–809.
    • OpenNeuro dataset ds004408, version 1.0.8 — doi:10.18112/openneuro.ds004408.v1.0.8
    • Dryad dataset — doi:10.5061/dryad.070jc

    Methods referenced above

    • Crosse, M. J., Di Liberto, G. M., Bednar, A., & Lalor, E. C. (2016). The Multivariate Temporal Response Function (mTRF) Toolbox: a MATLAB toolbox for relating neural signals to continuous stimuli. Frontiers in Human Neuroscience, 10, 604. — the reference implementation this library is measured against.
    • Gorman, K., Howell, J., & Wagner, M. (2011). Prosodylab-Aligner: a tool for forced alignment of laboratory speech. Canadian Acoustics, 39(3), 192–193. — produced the .TextGrid phoneme alignments shipped with the OpenNeuro release.
    • Lescroart, M. D., Stansbury, D. E., & Gallant, J. L. (2015). Fourier power, subjective distance, and object categories all provide plausible models of BOLD responses in scene-selective visual areas. Frontiers in Computational Neuroscience, 9, 135. — the variance partition of section 16.
    • de Heer, W. A., Huth, A. G., Griffiths, T. L., Gallant, J. L., & Theunissen, F. E. (2017). The hierarchical cortical organization of human speech processing. Journal of Neuroscience, 37(27), 6539–6557. — the variance partition of section 16.
    • Fox, J., & Monette, G. (1992). Generalized collinearity diagnostics. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 87(417), 178–183. — the GVIF reported in section 12.
    • Smith, S. M., & Nichols, T. E. (2009). Threshold-free cluster enhancement. NeuroImage, 44(1), 83–98. — the correction used in section 11.

    2 · Setup¶

    The only hard requirement beyond TRFlearn is MNE, which does the file I/O, the filtering and the sensor geometry.

    # ── Analysis configuration ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
FS           = 128                       # Hz, the rate the dataset ships at
WINDOW       = (-0.15, 0.45)             # TRF delay window, seconds
DELAY_MARGIN = 0.05                      # fitted wider, then trimmed (section 5)
GRID       = np.logspace(-8, 6, 36)    # ridge grid; the floor is deliberately low
N_FOLDS      = 5
N_PERMUTATIONS = 1024                    # for TFCE
N_RESAMPLES  = 2000                      # for the bootstrap
SEED         = 42

# Linear-phase FIR (firwin, Hamming window), its delay compensated: zero phase.
# Passband 1.5-14 Hz with 0.5 and 1 Hz transitions, so it is attenuated from 1 Hz
# and from 15 Hz on: the edges of the original study's Chebyshev filter.
BAND    = (1.5, 14.0)
FIR     = dict(method="fir", phase="zero", fir_design="firwin",
               fir_window="hamming", l_trans_bandwidth=0.5,
               h_trans_bandwidth=1.0)

USE_GPU = torch.cuda.is_available()

DATA_ROOT = Path.cwd().parent.parent / "LalorData" / "NaturalSpeechReferencedDryad"
SUBJECTS  = sorted(int(m.group(1))
                   for p in (DATA_ROOT / "eeg_ica").glob("sub*")
                   if p.is_dir() and (m := re.fullmatch(r"sub(\d+)", p.name)))
SEGMENTS  = list(range(1, 21))

# Part II's predictors come from the OpenNeuro release's forced-aligned transcripts.
PREDICTORS = ["Envelope", "Phonemes", "Words"]
TEXTGRIDS  = DATA_ROOT.parent / "NaturalSpeech_VOpenNeuro" / "stimuli"
SILENCE    = {"", "sil", "sp"}               # TextGrid labels that are not speech
print(f"Subjects  : {len(SUBJECTS)} -> {SUBJECTS}")
print(f"Segments  : {len(SEGMENTS)} per subject")

    3 · Loading — and why the targets are mne.Raw objects¶

    TRFData accepts its targets as plain arrays or as mne.Raw, one per segment. The Raw route is preferable here and not merely for convenience: channel names, channel types and the montage travel with the data into TRFData.info.

    That matters more than it looks. Without a montage, TRFGroup.tfce has no channel adjacency to build and falls back to treating the 128 electrodes as independent — which would quietly invalidate the group statistics later on. Since these .fif files already carry biosemi128 embedded, passing Raw gets it right with no montage bookkeeping at all, and every Evoked-based plot works immediately.

    Note that all three predictors are built here, including the two Part I will not use.

    In [3]:
    Copied! 
    def onset_train(segment: int, tier: str, n: int) -> np.ndarray:
    """A unit impulse where each labelled interval of a TextGrid tier starts."""
    text = (TEXTGRIDS / f"audio{segment:02d}.TextGrid").read_text("utf-8")
    block = text.split(f'name = "{tier}"')[1].split("item [")[0]
    starts = np.array([
        float(start) for start, label in re.findall(
            r'xmin = ([\d.]+)\s*xmax = [\d.]+\s*text = "([^"]*)"', block
        )
        if label.strip().lower() not in SILENCE
    ])
    index = np.round(starts * FS).astype(int)
    train = np.zeros((n, 1))
    train[index[index < n], 0] = 1.0
    return train


def load_aligned_segment(subject: int, segment: int):
    """One run: band-passed EEG as `mne.Raw`, plus the three stimulus predictors."""
    raw = mne.io.read_raw_fif(
        DATA_ROOT / "eeg_ica" / f"sub{subject:02d}" / f"eeg_segment{segment:02d}.fif",
        preload=True, verbose="error"
    )

    # Zero-phase FIR: no peak is shifted. A causal filter would delay every peak
    # and corrupt the latencies we care about.
    raw.filter(l_freq=BAND[0], h_freq=BAND[1], **FIR, verbose="error")

    env = np.load(DATA_ROOT / "stimuli" / "envelope" /
                  f"envelope_segment{segment:02d}.npy").astype(np.float64)

    # The envelope runs 7-11 samples longer than the EEG; trim both to the common
    # length so every design-matrix row means the same instant on both sides.
    n = min(len(env), raw.n_times)
    raw.crop(tmax=(n - 1) / FS, verbose="error")

    predictors = {
        "Envelope": env[:n].reshape(-1, 1),
        "Phonemes": onset_train(segment, "phones", n),     # used in Part II
        "Words": onset_train(segment, "words", n),         # idem
    }
    return raw, predictors


def build_subject(subject: int, segments=SEGMENTS) -> TRFData:
    """A partitioned `TRFData` for one subject: 20 segments, three predictors."""
    raws, features = [], {name: [] for name in PREDICTORS}
    for seg in segments:
        raw, predictors = load_aligned_segment(subject, seg)
        raws.append(raw)
        for name, x in predictors.items():
            features[name].append(x)

    data = TRFData(
        features=features,
        y=raws,                      # montage + channel names ride along
        sample_rate=FS,
        use_gpu=USE_GPU
    )
    # Folds are a property of the data, not of the model.
    # Block-stratified so each fold draws from every segment instead of being one
    # contiguous chunk.
    return data.create_partitions(n_folds=N_FOLDS, stratify_by_segment=True)
    def onset_train(segment: int, tier: str, n: int) -> np.ndarray: """A unit impulse where each labelled interval of a TextGrid tier starts.""" text = (TEXTGRIDS / f"audio{segment:02d}.TextGrid").read_text("utf-8") block = text.split(f'name = "{tier}"')[1].split("item [")[0] starts = np.array([ float(start) for start, label in re.findall( r'xmin = ([\d.]+)\s*xmax = [\d.]+\s*text = "([^"]*)"', block ) if label.strip().lower() not in SILENCE ]) index = np.round(starts * FS).astype(int) train = np.zeros((n, 1)) train[index[index < n], 0] = 1.0 return train def load_aligned_segment(subject: int, segment: int): """One run: band-passed EEG as `mne.Raw`, plus the three stimulus predictors.""" raw = mne.io.read_raw_fif( DATA_ROOT / "eeg_ica" / f"sub{subject:02d}" / f"eeg_segment{segment:02d}.fif", preload=True, verbose="error" ) # Zero-phase FIR: no peak is shifted. A causal filter would delay every peak # and corrupt the latencies we care about. raw.filter(l_freq=BAND[0], h_freq=BAND[1], **FIR, verbose="error") env = np.load(DATA_ROOT / "stimuli" / "envelope" / f"envelope_segment{segment:02d}.npy").astype(np.float64) # The envelope runs 7-11 samples longer than the EEG; trim both to the common # length so every design-matrix row means the same instant on both sides. n = min(len(env), raw.n_times) raw.crop(tmax=(n - 1) / FS, verbose="error") predictors = { "Envelope": env[:n].reshape(-1, 1), "Phonemes": onset_train(segment, "phones", n), # used in Part II "Words": onset_train(segment, "words", n), # idem } return raw, predictors def build_subject(subject: int, segments=SEGMENTS) -> TRFData: """A partitioned `TRFData` for one subject: 20 segments, three predictors.""" raws, features = [], {name: [] for name in PREDICTORS} for seg in segments: raw, predictors = load_aligned_segment(subject, seg) raws.append(raw) for name, x in predictors.items(): features[name].append(x) data = TRFData( features=features, y=raws, # montage + channel names ride along sample_rate=FS, use_gpu=USE_GPU ) # Folds are a property of the data, not of the model. # Block-stratified so each fold draws from every segment instead of being one # contiguous chunk. return data.create_partitions(n_folds=N_FOLDS, stratify_by_segment=True)

    What one run looks like¶

    In [4]:
    Copied! 
    raw0, predictors0 = load_aligned_segment(SUBJECTS[4], 1)
t = np.arange(raw0.n_times) / FS
sl = slice(int(20 * FS), int(30 * FS))          # a 10-second window

fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(10, 5.5), sharex=True,
                         gridspec_kw=dict(height_ratios=[1, 0.6, 1.6]))
axes[0].plot(t[sl], predictors0["Envelope"][sl, 0], color="C0", lw=1.4)
axes[0].set_ylabel("Envelope")
for row, (name, colour) in enumerate([("Phonemes", "C1"), ("Words", "C2")]):
    onsets = t[sl][predictors0[name][sl, 0] > 0]
    axes[1].vlines(onsets, 1 - row, 1.8 - row, color=colour, lw=1.4)
axes[1].set_yticks([1.4, 0.4], ["Phonemes", "Words"])
picks = ["A1", "B22", "B21"]
data_uv = raw0.get_data(picks=picks)[:, sl] * 1e6
for i, (ch, trace) in enumerate(zip(picks, data_uv)):
    axes[2].plot(t[sl], trace + i * 60, lw=.9, label=ch)
axes[2].set(xlabel="Time (s)", ylabel="EEG (a.u., offset)")
axes[2].legend(ncol=3, fontsize=8, loc="upper right")
for a in axes:
    a.grid(alpha=.3)
axes[0].set_title(f"sub{SUBJECTS[4]:02d}, run 01 — {raw0.n_times / FS:.0f} s total, "
                  f"showing 20-30 s")
plt.tight_layout()

seconds = raw0.n_times / FS
print(f"EEG   {raw0.n_times} samples x {len(raw0.ch_names)} channels, "
      f"montage: {raw0.get_montage() is not None}")
print("stim  " + ", ".join(f"{name} {x.shape}" for name, x in predictors0.items()))
print(f"rate  {predictors0['Phonemes'].sum() / seconds:.1f} phonemes/s, "
      f"{predictors0['Words'].sum() / seconds:.1f} words/s")
del raw0


def rise_lag_ms(segment: int) -> float:
    """The delay at which the envelope's rise best follows phoneme onsets."""
    env = np.load(DATA_ROOT / "stimuli" / "envelope"
                  / f"envelope_segment{segment:02d}.npy")
    rise = np.maximum(np.diff(env, prepend=env[0]), 0.0)
    phonemes = onset_train(segment, "phones", len(env))[:, 0]
    lags = np.arange(-FS // 4, FS // 4 + 1)
    score = [np.dot(np.roll(rise, -lag), phonemes) for lag in lags]
    return 1e3 * lags[int(np.argmax(score))] / FS


lags_ms = [rise_lag_ms(seg) for seg in SEGMENTS]
print(f"the envelope rises {np.min(lags_ms):.0f} to {np.max(lags_ms):.0f} ms after "
      f"a phoneme onset, over the {len(SEGMENTS)} runs")
    raw0, predictors0 = load_aligned_segment(SUBJECTS[4], 1) t = np.arange(raw0.n_times) / FS sl = slice(int(20 * FS), int(30 * FS)) # a 10-second window fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(10, 5.5), sharex=True, gridspec_kw=dict(height_ratios=[1, 0.6, 1.6])) axes[0].plot(t[sl], predictors0["Envelope"][sl, 0], color="C0", lw=1.4) axes[0].set_ylabel("Envelope") for row, (name, colour) in enumerate([("Phonemes", "C1"), ("Words", "C2")]): onsets = t[sl][predictors0[name][sl, 0] > 0] axes[1].vlines(onsets, 1 - row, 1.8 - row, color=colour, lw=1.4) axes[1].set_yticks([1.4, 0.4], ["Phonemes", "Words"]) picks = ["A1", "B22", "B21"] data_uv = raw0.get_data(picks=picks)[:, sl] * 1e6 for i, (ch, trace) in enumerate(zip(picks, data_uv)): axes[2].plot(t[sl], trace + i * 60, lw=.9, label=ch) axes[2].set(xlabel="Time (s)", ylabel="EEG (a.u., offset)") axes[2].legend(ncol=3, fontsize=8, loc="upper right") for a in axes: a.grid(alpha=.3) axes[0].set_title(f"sub{SUBJECTS[4]:02d}, run 01 — {raw0.n_times / FS:.0f} s total, " f"showing 20-30 s") plt.tight_layout() seconds = raw0.n_times / FS print(f"EEG {raw0.n_times} samples x {len(raw0.ch_names)} channels, " f"montage: {raw0.get_montage() is not None}") print("stim " + ", ".join(f"{name} {x.shape}" for name, x in predictors0.items())) print(f"rate {predictors0['Phonemes'].sum() / seconds:.1f} phonemes/s, " f"{predictors0['Words'].sum() / seconds:.1f} words/s") del raw0 def rise_lag_ms(segment: int) -> float: """The delay at which the envelope's rise best follows phoneme onsets.""" env = np.load(DATA_ROOT / "stimuli" / "envelope" / f"envelope_segment{segment:02d}.npy") rise = np.maximum(np.diff(env, prepend=env[0]), 0.0) phonemes = onset_train(segment, "phones", len(env))[:, 0] lags = np.arange(-FS // 4, FS // 4 + 1) score = [np.dot(np.roll(rise, -lag), phonemes) for lag in lags] return 1e3 * lags[int(np.argmax(score))] / FS lags_ms = [rise_lag_ms(seg) for seg in SEGMENTS] print(f"the envelope rises {np.min(lags_ms):.0f} to {np.max(lags_ms):.0f} ms after " f"a phoneme onset, over the {len(SEGMENTS)} runs") 
    EEG   22729 samples x 128 channels, montage: True
stim  Envelope (22729, 1), Phonemes (22729, 1), Words (22729, 1)
rate  10.2 phonemes/s, 3.3 words/s

    the envelope rises 16 to 16 ms after a phoneme onset, over the 20 runs

    The three predictors are related. Every word begins with a phoneme, so the word train is a subset of the phoneme train, and both sit where the envelope tends to rise. That overlap is what makes Part I clean and Part II interesting; section 12 quantifies it.

    The last line is the alignment check. The transcript and the envelope come from different releases, and the envelope is cut to the audio: had the transcript been offset from it, the lag at which the envelope rises after a phoneme onset would differ from run to run, rather than be the same short delay in all twenty.

    4 · The container holds candidates; the model chooses¶

    TRFData is a container of named candidate features, not a fixed design. It holds everything that might be modelled, and each model then names the subset it wants. That separation is what the next two parts are built on: the container below carries Envelope, Phonemes and Words, Part I fits models that ask only for Envelope, and Part II reuses the very same container to ask for all three.

    Part I — The envelope TRF¶

    One predictor, Envelope, selected out of a container that holds three. Everything from here to section 11 uses that single-feature model.

    5 · One subject, and what the choices actually do¶

    cv="pooled" is TRFlearn's default and the recommended one: for each held-out fold a model is fitted on the pooled complement, so nothing in the reported score was seen while fitting. gridsearchCV searches λ on an inner split of the training data and then refits at the winner — the refit is not optional at the cohort level, so a reported kernel is always one that was actually fitted.

    Two settings deserve to be spelled out rather than left at their defaults.

    delay_margin=0.05. Ridge regression rings at the edges of the delay window: the first and last lags have no neighbours on one side, and the penalty pulls them toward zero in a way that bends the kernel where it should simply end. Fitting 50 ms wider on each side and then trimming the margin off before predicting moves that artefact outside the window you actually look at. The kernel comes back at the requested −150–450 ms; the fit that produced it was wider.

    The metric. The library chooses λ on R² by default; Pearson correlation is what the TRF literature reports. One search can give both: extra_metrics scores more metrics on the same held-out samples as the one that chooses, and they are reported, never choosing. Below, λ is chosen on R² with Pearson's r and RMSE beside it. The parameters are written out in full so the choices are legible, even where they match the defaults.

    In [6]:
    Copied! 
    FEATURE = ["Envelope"]          # one name, out of the three the container holds
METRICS = ["r2", "Pearson", "RMSE"]

model = TRFModel(
    data, FEATURE, WINDOW,
    cv="pooled",                     # k-fold; the default paradigm
    solver="ridge",                  # the default
    feature_preprocess="Standardize",  # the default: z-scored with train stats
    target_preprocess="Standardize",   # idem
    delay_margin=DELAY_MARGIN,       # fit wider, trim after
)
best_regularization, _ = model.gridsearchCV(
    GRID,
    metric="r2",                          # chooses λ; the default
    extra_metrics=METRICS[1:],            # scored beside it, never choosing
    metric_aggregation_function="mean",   # how folds are pooled; the default
    metric_limit_percentage=None,         # None = simply take the best λ
    inner_train_cutoff=0.8,               # the default inner split
    validation_plot=False,
    run_fit=True,                         # refit at the winner
)

scores = [model.metric_] + [model.extra_metrics_[m] for m in METRICS[1:]]
print(f"λ = {best_regularization:.4g} | "
      + " | ".join(f"{name} {float(s.mean()):.4f}"
                   for name, s in zip(["R²", "r", "RMSE"], scores)))
    FEATURE = ["Envelope"] # one name, out of the three the container holds METRICS = ["r2", "Pearson", "RMSE"] model = TRFModel( data, FEATURE, WINDOW, cv="pooled", # k-fold; the default paradigm solver="ridge", # the default feature_preprocess="Standardize", # the default: z-scored with train stats target_preprocess="Standardize", # idem delay_margin=DELAY_MARGIN, # fit wider, trim after ) best_regularization, _ = model.gridsearchCV( GRID, metric="r2", # chooses λ; the default extra_metrics=METRICS[1:], # scored beside it, never choosing metric_aggregation_function="mean", # how folds are pooled; the default metric_limit_percentage=None, # None = simply take the best λ inner_train_cutoff=0.8, # the default inner split validation_plot=False, run_fit=True, # refit at the winner ) scores = [model.metric_] + [model.extra_metrics_[m] for m in METRICS[1:]] print(f"λ = {best_regularization:.4g} | " + " | ".join(f"{name} {float(s.mean()):.4f}" for name, s in zip(["R²", "r", "RMSE"], scores))) 
    λ = 0.1585 | R² 0.0046 | r 0.0650 | RMSE 0.9982

    Why the literature reports Pearson, and the library chooses on R². Correlation is scale-invariant: a response can be real, correctly timed, and still amount to a few hundredths of correlation without being penalised for its small amplitude, which makes it the number to report and to compare across studies. The same invariance makes it a poor judge of λ. Ridge shrinks the kernel, and shrinking it scales its prediction: correlation barely sees that, while R² scores the prediction's amplitude as well as its shape, so a search on R² keeps the kernel's size closer to what the data support. R² wins when the kernel is the result — its amplitude, a group average, a comparison between subjects or conditions. Pearson wins when prediction accuracy is the result, and on a short or noisy recording, where the extra shrinkage it tolerates keeps a weak kernel from being mostly noise. RMSE is the only registered metric where lower is better, so the search flips its sign internally; and held-out R² can be negative, which is information rather than failure.

    Here the three metrics agree. Every curve below is flat from the bottom of the grid up to λ ≈ 0.1 and only then turns: with one predictor, 90 design columns and nearly half a million samples, the normal equations are well conditioned and the penalty has almost nothing to do until it starts smoothing the kernel. On such a plateau a plain argmax chooses between near-ties, and a subject whose curve never turns settles on the bottom of the grid. That says the penalty is not what limits that fit, which is why section 9 checks the two grid endpoints separately. When a smoother kernel is wanted, metric_limit_percentage takes the largest λ within a tolerance of the best instead.

    validation_plot — the λ search made visible. One row per metric, the R² that chose λ and the two reported beside it, with the selection marked; below them, the kernel at every λ on the grid. Read together, the curves say which λ won and the stack says what regularisation was doing to the shape on the way there.

    This is where the paragraph above becomes something you can see rather than take on trust: the three curves have the same shape — flat over the bottom of the grid, a barely visible optimum where the plateau ends, and a fall beyond it (a rise, for RMSE) as the penalty starts to shrink the kernel. Mind the axes, which each panel scales on its own: R² falls to zero, r loses about a tenth of its value, and RMSE moves in the third decimal. The stack shows what that fall costs: the peaks lower and widen as λ grows. A curve that never turned around, climbing toward the largest λ on offer, would be the signature of a selection rule that wants no model at all; none of these does.

    In [7]:
    docs-figure:validation_plot_metrics
    Copied! 
    model.validation_plot(METRICS, show=True);
    model.validation_plot(METRICS, show=True);

    plot_metric_topomap — the same model scored on the scalp, once per metric. R² and Pearson should show structure, and structure in the right place: fronto-central, where an auditory response belongs. They share their shape, since on any one channel both grow with how much of it the kernel predicts. Held-out correlations of a few hundredths per channel are normal for single-trial continuous speech.

    6 · Diagnosing the design¶

    Before trusting a kernel, ask whether the design that produced it was well posed. model.diagnostics() answers that. It is computed on demand rather than during fitting — it costs a full extra pass over the design — and it needs the fitted λ, because the condition number it reports is that of the regularised normal matrix, which is the matrix actually inverted.

    quantity what it says
    condition_number how close the regularised system is to singular; > 1e6 warns
    effective_rank participation ratio of the unregularised design — how many directions genuinely carry variance
    vif generalised VIF per feature block (Fox & Monette), so collinearity within the lag axis is not counted as a problem
    vif_columns / vif_aliased per design column; inf marks exact linear dependence
    In [9]:
    Copied! 
    diag = model.diagnostics(vif=True, criteria=True)

print(f"condition number : {diag['condition_number']:.3e}")
print(f"effective rank   : {diag['effective_rank']:.1f} "
      f"of {np.size(diag['vif_columns'])} design columns")
print(f"aliased columns  : {np.size(diag['vif_aliased'])}")
print(f"GVIF             : {np.atleast_1d(diag['vif'])}   <- one block, nothing to share with")
    diag = model.diagnostics(vif=True, criteria=True) print(f"condition number : {diag['condition_number']:.3e}") print(f"effective rank : {diag['effective_rank']:.1f} " f"of {np.size(diag['vif_columns'])} design columns") print(f"aliased columns : {np.size(diag['vif_aliased'])}") print(f"GVIF : {np.atleast_1d(diag['vif'])} <- one block, nothing to share with")
    condition number : 1.677e+02
effective rank   : 6.9 of 90 design columns
aliased columns  : 0
GVIF             : [nan]   <- one block, nothing to share with

    Two of the three say something here, and the third says nothing by construction.

    The effective rank is far below the column count. About seven effective directions out of 90 design columns is not a defect — it is what a lagged low-frequency predictor is. Neighbouring delays of a slowly varying signal are nearly the same regressor, so the design's variance concentrates into a handful of directions. This is precisely why ridge is not optional: the unregularised problem is close to singular, and the penalty is what makes it solvable.

    The condition number is of the regularised matrix — the one actually inverted. It reflects the problem after λ has done its work, which is why the diagnostic needs a fitted λ and refuses to run before one exists.

    The GVIF is empty, and has to be. It measures how much a feature block duplicates the other blocks, and a single-block design has no other blocks. This is not a limitation to work around; it is the diagnostic correctly reporting that the question does not apply yet. In Part II it will.

    7 · The plotting API on a single subject¶

    Every figure below is a method on the fitted object, returns its Figure, and accepts save_path. Models, cohorts and individual subjects share one API, so nothing here has to be relearned at the group level.

    Kernel amplitudes are in µV per unit of the envelope. The model was fitted on standardised data, and its figures undo that, coef_ · σ_EEG / σ_x (kernel_units="original", the default). The envelope has no physical unit, so the axis says x units; feature_units names one when a feature has it. kernel_units="standardized" draws the coefficients as fitted instead, in standard deviations of the EEG per standard deviation of the envelope.

    plot — MNE's butterfly of the kernel, with a black channel-mean and a ±1 SD band over the per-channel traces.

    8 · Fitting the cohort¶

    TRFGroup declares the model spec once, without data, fits it per subject, keeps only the minimal per-subject record — kernels, held-out metric, selected λ, diagnostics — and discards each full model. That is what makes 17 subjects × 60 minutes tractable in a notebook.

    Two flags must be set before fitting and cannot be recovered afterwards, precisely because each subject's model is discarded:

    • criteria=True — records AIC/BIC, which Part II's compare_to reports beside the cross-validated R²;
    • diagnostics=True — records the design report from section 6 for every subject.

    One λ for the whole cohort. Each subject's own search would pick its own λ, and a noisier subject picks a larger one and is shrunk more — so with a λ per subject, part of any difference between subjects is a difference in noise. The cohort below shares one, chosen by leave-one-subject-out: the λ at which the other subjects' average kernel best predicts each subject, scored on R². It keeps every subject's kernels at every λ — a couple of MB per subject with one predictor — and with them the curves every other strategy reads, so the figure after the search can show what those would have picked.

    Sharing takes two passes: search_subject on every subject, share_regularization(), then fit_subject on every subject at the shared λ. The second pass is there for bootstrap, diagnostics and criteria, which need each subject's data at the final λ; without them, share_regularization() alone fills every record from the kernels leave-one-out kept.

    In [14]:
    Copied! 
    envelope_group = TRFGroup(
    ["Envelope"], default_window=WINDOW,
    cv="pooled", solver="ridge",
    delay_margin=DELAY_MARGIN,
    regularization_grid=GRID,
    metric="r2", extra_metrics=["Pearson"],    # R² chooses λ, r is reported
    regularization_strategy="leave-one-out",   # one λ for the whole cohort
    diagnostics=True, criteria=True,
    bootstrap=True, n_resamples=N_RESAMPLES, random_state=SEED,
)
print("spec:", envelope_group.features, "| window:", WINDOW,
      "| margin:", DELAY_MARGIN, "s")
    envelope_group = TRFGroup( ["Envelope"], default_window=WINDOW, cv="pooled", solver="ridge", delay_margin=DELAY_MARGIN, regularization_grid=GRID, metric="r2", extra_metrics=["Pearson"], # R² chooses λ, r is reported regularization_strategy="leave-one-out", # one λ for the whole cohort diagnostics=True, criteria=True, bootstrap=True, n_resamples=N_RESAMPLES, random_state=SEED, ) print("spec:", envelope_group.features, "| window:", WINDOW, "| margin:", DELAY_MARGIN, "s")

    Copied! 
    # Pass 1: each subject's search, and its kernels at every λ for leave-one-out.
for sub in SUBJECTS:
    envelope_group.search_subject(build_subject(sub), f"sub{sub:02d}")

# What each strategy would share; the last call is the one the cohort keeps.
for strategy in ("median", "mean-curve", "leave-one-out"):
    print(f"{strategy:14s} λ = {envelope_group.share_regularization(strategy):.4g}")
    # Pass 1: each subject's search, and its kernels at every λ for leave-one-out. for sub in SUBJECTS: envelope_group.search_subject(build_subject(sub), f"sub{sub:02d}") # What each strategy would share; the last call is the one the cohort keeps. for strategy in ("median", "mean-curve", "leave-one-out"): print(f"{strategy:14s} λ = {envelope_group.share_regularization(strategy):.4g}")
    median         λ = 2.512
mean-curve     λ = 1
leave-one-out  λ = 1

    plot_regularization_search — the cohort's counterpart of validation_plot. Each subject's validation curve is drawn in grey and the leave-one-out curve on top, one row per metric; the strip below marks the λ each subject's own search chose, and each strategy draws a vertical line at the λ it picks, the shared one in red.

    Leave-one-out and the mean curve agree on λ = 1 — the mean curve's line is hidden under the red one — and the median of the subjects' own choices sits one step above, at 2.5. On their own the subjects would have spread over more than two decades, from 0.16 to 40, and the leave-one-out curve peaks in the middle of that spread. It also sits below the average of the subjects' own curves: the other subjects' average kernel predicts a subject less well than that subject's own kernel does. That gap is the cost of one kernel for a cohort, and the leave-one-out curve is the one that measures it.

    Prediction per subject, and the cohort's landmarks¶

    The figure below is descriptive housekeeping: how well the model predicts for each person at the shared λ. Prediction accuracy varying by a factor of a few across subjects is normal.

    The subjects' own λ, from the first pass, are still worth checking at the two grid endpoints, because those mean opposite things. Landing on the ceiling is a genuine warning: the search wants more regularisation than the grid offers, which is a model being shrunk toward nothing. Landing on the floor is the flat-curve situation from section 5: a design well enough conditioned that ridge has little left to do. On R² no subject lands on either here. Their spread, more than two decades, is what the shared λ removes: with a λ per subject, a noisier subject would be shrunk more, and its kernel would come out smaller for that reason alone.

    The final block reads the classic auditory landmarks — P1, N1, P2 — off the channel-averaged group kernel. This is the notebook's real validation step: if those latencies land near the values reported for this paradigm, then the whole chain — filtering, alignment, folds, the λ search, the margin trimming — is behaving.

    In [19]:
    Copied!

    np.asarray(envelope_group.results(f"sub{s:02d}")["extra_metrics"]["Pearson"]).reshape(-1)
    for s in SUBJECTS
])
x = np.arange(len(SUBJECTS))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.6))
ax.bar(x, r_by_sub.mean(1), color="C0", label="channel mean")
ax.plot(x, r_by_sub.max(1), "o", color="C3", ms=4, label="best channel")
ax.set_xticks(x, [f"{s:02d}" for s in SUBJECTS], fontsize=7)
ax.set(xlabel="subject", ylabel="held-out r",
       title="Prediction accuracy at the shared λ")
ax.legend(fontsize=8); ax.grid(alpha=.3, axis="y")
plt.tight_layout()

print(f"r across cohort : {r_by_sub.mean():.4f} "
      f"(best channel per subject: {r_by_sub.max(1).mean():.4f})")

on_floor   = (own <= GRID[0]).sum()
on_ceiling = (own >= GRID[-1]).sum()
print(f"own λ on the grid floor  : {on_floor} of {len(SUBJECTS)}"
      + ("" if on_floor == 0 else
         "   (flat metric curve; the penalty is not the limiting factor — section 5)"))
print(f"own λ on the grid ceiling: {on_ceiling} of {len(SUBJECTS)}"
      + ("" if on_ceiling == 0 else "   <-- the model is being shrunk away; widen GRID"))

delays = np.asarray(envelope_group.results(f"sub{SUBJECTS[0]:02d}")["delays"]["Envelope"])
t_ms   = delays / FS * 1e3
kernel = np.asarray(ga["Envelope"]["mean"])              # (channels, d, delays)
curve  = kernel.reshape(-1, kernel.shape[-1]).mean(axis=0)

early, late = (t_ms >= -50) & (t_ms <= 90), (t_ms >= 0) & (t_ms <= 300)
print(f"\ndelays kept     : {t_ms[0]:.0f} to {t_ms[-1]:.0f} ms "
      f"({len(t_ms)} lags, margin already trimmed)")
print(f"group TRF peaks : P1 {t_ms[early][curve[early].argmax()]:.0f} ms, "
      f"N1 {t_ms[late][curve[late].argmin()]:.0f} ms, "
      f"P2 {t_ms[late][curve[late].argmax()]:.0f} ms"
      f"   [literature: ~25 / ~80 / ~140 ms]")
    r_by_sub = np.stack([ np.asarray(envelope_group.results(f"sub{s:02d}")["extra_metrics"]["Pearson"]).reshape(-1) for s in SUBJECTS ]) x = np.arange(len(SUBJECTS)) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.6)) ax.bar(x, r_by_sub.mean(1), color="C0", label="channel mean") ax.plot(x, r_by_sub.max(1), "o", color="C3", ms=4, label="best channel") ax.set_xticks(x, [f"{s:02d}" for s in SUBJECTS], fontsize=7) ax.set(xlabel="subject", ylabel="held-out r", title="Prediction accuracy at the shared λ") ax.legend(fontsize=8); ax.grid(alpha=.3, axis="y") plt.tight_layout() print(f"r across cohort : {r_by_sub.mean():.4f} " f"(best channel per subject: {r_by_sub.max(1).mean():.4f})") on_floor = (own <= GRID[0]).sum() on_ceiling = (own >= GRID[-1]).sum() print(f"own λ on the grid floor : {on_floor} of {len(SUBJECTS)}" + ("" if on_floor == 0 else " (flat metric curve; the penalty is not the limiting factor — section 5)")) print(f"own λ on the grid ceiling: {on_ceiling} of {len(SUBJECTS)}" + ("" if on_ceiling == 0 else " <-- the model is being shrunk away; widen GRID")) delays = np.asarray(envelope_group.results(f"sub{SUBJECTS[0]:02d}")["delays"]["Envelope"]) t_ms = delays / FS * 1e3 kernel = np.asarray(ga["Envelope"]["mean"]) # (channels, d, delays) curve = kernel.reshape(-1, kernel.shape[-1]).mean(axis=0) early, late = (t_ms >= -50) & (t_ms <= 90), (t_ms >= 0) & (t_ms <= 300) print(f"\ndelays kept : {t_ms[0]:.0f} to {t_ms[-1]:.0f} ms " f"({len(t_ms)} lags, margin already trimmed)") print(f"group TRF peaks : P1 {t_ms[early][curve[early].argmax()]:.0f} ms, " f"N1 {t_ms[late][curve[late].argmin()]:.0f} ms, " f"P2 {t_ms[late][curve[late].argmax()]:.0f} ms" f" [literature: ~25 / ~80 / ~140 ms]")

    N1 and P2 land where the literature puts them; the P1 does not. It peaks just before zero rather than ~25 ms after it. A zero-phase filter spreads every deflection to both sides in time (section 1), and the P1 — small, and right before the large N1 — is the most exposed to that spread. The rest of the chain is behaving.

    Design diagnostics across the cohort¶

    Section 6 diagnosed one subject, which cannot say much on its own. The question a cohort asks is whether this subject's design is the odd one out, so summary()["diagnostics"] reports the spread across subjects and names anyone carrying an exact dependency. aliased_subjects should be empty; if it is not, those subjects have redundant design columns and their kernels are not identified in those directions.

    10 · Bootstrap distributions per subject¶

    bootstrap=True resamples folds with replacement at fit time, giving each subject a distribution for its held-out metric rather than a single number. plot_bootstrap draws one violin per subject with the observed value, a percentile interval and the cohort mean.

    This is the figure that separates "the cohort average is positive" from "the cohort average is positive and most individuals are individually credible" — a distinction a bar chart of means cannot make.

    11 · Group inference with TFCE¶

    The question is whether the cohort's kernel departs from zero, controlling the family-wise error over the whole delay × channel grid — 128 channels times the delay axis is a lot of opportunities to find something.

    group.tfce(spec) wraps mne.stats.spatio_temporal_cluster_1samp_test and builds the full adjacency lattice (delays × channel neighbourhood) from the montage carried in TRFData.info. This is where section 3's choice to pass mne.Raw pays off: without that montage the channel adjacency degrades to the identity, every electrode becomes an island, and the correction goes wrong without raising anything. TRFlearn warns when it falls back, so a cell with no warning under it is the check that the correction used real sensor neighbourhoods.

    Why TFCE rather than cluster mass. Under cluster mass the p-value belongs to the cluster, not to any delay or channel inside it, so "this cluster is significant" is the only honest statement and reading a latency off its edges is unsupported. TFCE returns a genuine per-point p-value, which is what makes the shaded figures below interpretable.

    What to expect: a fraction of the grid significant, concentrated around the N1 and the P2 over fronto-central sensors. Nothing significant, or everything significant, would both be signs that something upstream is wrong.

    In [22]:
    Copied! 
    t_obs, pvals = envelope_group.tfce("Envelope", n_permutations=N_PERMUTATIONS,
                                   seed=SEED, n_jobs=-1)
sig = pvals < 0.05
print(f"Envelope: t_obs {t_obs.shape} | {sig.sum():,} of {sig.size:,} points "
      f"p < .05 ({100 * sig.mean():.1f} %) | min p = {pvals.min():.4g}")
    t_obs, pvals = envelope_group.tfce("Envelope", n_permutations=N_PERMUTATIONS, seed=SEED, n_jobs=-1) sig = pvals < 0.05 print(f"Envelope: t_obs {t_obs.shape} | {sig.sum():,} of {sig.size:,} points " f"p < .05 ({100 * sig.mean():.1f} %) | min p = {pvals.min():.4g}")

    Part II — Adding phonemes and words¶

    The container has carried Phonemes and Words since section 3 without any model asking for them. Now one does.

    The point of this part is not that three predictors are better than one. It is that adding correlated predictors changes what the first one means, and that TRFlearn gives you the tools to see that happening rather than discover it later: a between-block collinearity diagnostic that was empty in Part I, a comparison that asks whether the new predictors earn their place, and a partition of the explained variance that says what each one explains alone and what they explain alike.

    12 · Three blocks, and a diagnostic that now has something to say¶

    The same container, the same window, the same margin — only the feature list changes.

    In [27]:
    Copied! 
    joint_model = TRFModel(
    data, PREDICTORS, WINDOW,
    cv="pooled", solver="ridge", delay_margin=DELAY_MARGIN,
)

    GRID, extra_metrics=["Pearson"], validation_plot=False, run_fit=True,
)
joint_diag = joint_model.diagnostics(vif=True, criteria=True)

print(f"selected λ       : {joint_regularization:.4g}")

        ("R²", joint_model.metric_, model.metric_),
        ("r ", joint_model.extra_metrics_["Pearson"], model.extra_metrics_["Pearson"])]:

      f"{np.size(joint_diag['vif_columns'])} columns")

    Now the GVIF says something. A value of 1.0 would mean a block shares nothing with the others. The envelope's, 1.03, is close to it: a smooth amplitude contour and two trains of impulses have little in common once each is lagged. Phonemes and words, at 1.22, share with each other, as they must — every word onset is a phoneme onset. These values quantify a known overlap rather than warn about an unknown one, and read together with vif_aliased, which is empty, they say the blocks are correlated but not redundant. An exact dependency would be the serious case, because then the split between the blocks would be arbitrary rather than merely uncertain.

    13 · What the new predictors do to the envelope¶

    The Envelope kernel is not the same object in the two models. Fitted alone it absorbs everything the envelope correlates with; fitted alongside other blocks it keeps only what they do not already explain, and the variance they share gets divided between the blocks. How much that changes the kernel is what the GVIF above predicts. At 1.03 the envelope shares almost nothing with the onsets, so its P1–N1–P2 should come out of the joint model nearly as it went in — and below, it does. The phoneme and word kernels are the ones that share, and how the response at a word onset is split between them is the joint model's choice.

    The practical consequence holds either way: a TRF latency quoted without naming the model that produced it means nothing. Here the envelope's survives because nothing else in the model can predict in its place; with a predictor that could, such as the envelope's own derivative, it would not.

    In [28]:
    Copied! 
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.6), sharey=True)

for ax, (title, m, specs) in zip(axes, [
        ("Envelope alone", model, ["Envelope"]),
        ("Envelope + Phonemes + Words", joint_model, PREDICTORS)]):
    # `to_evoked` hands back the kernel as an mne.Evoked per feature: response
    # channels stay channels, the delays become the time axis (and may be
    # negative). It is also the bridge to the whole MNE plotting toolbox. Its
    # kernels are as fitted, in standard deviations, unlike the figures above:
    # the one unit in which an envelope and an onset kernel can share an axis.
    evokeds = m.to_evoked()
    for spec in specs:
        ev = evokeds[spec]
        ax.plot(ev.times * 1e3, ev.data.mean(axis=0), lw=2, label=spec)

    ax.axhline(0, color=".6", lw=.8)

axes[0].set_ylabel(r"Coefficient ($\sigma_{EEG}/\sigma_x$)")
plt.tight_layout();

    14 · The joint cohort¶

    The same 17 subjects, the same loading path, a different spec — and one more flag, variance_partition=True, which section 16 reads: in the second pass every subject also fits each of the seven subsets of the three predictors, at the shared λ and on its own folds. This time the three ways of sharing λ agree, on 0.40, one step of the grid below the envelope cohort's.

    15 · Do phonemes and words earn their place?¶

    TFCE asks whether a kernel differs from zero. A different question is which model spec describes the cohort better. compare_to answers it first by the cross-validated R²: both cohorts stored every subject's held-out score, and predictors that bring only noise lower it. That is one number per subject, tested across subjects with a signed-rank test, so neither the autocorrelation of the samples nor the correlation between channels enters the test.

    With criteria=True on both cohorts it also gives the in-sample answer, by AIC and BIC, under the same keys. Every delta is oriented the same way: positive favours other, here the joint cohort. That is the opposite of permutation_test_contrast, where a positive t_obs favours self.

    In [33]:
    Copied! 
    table = envelope_group.compare_to(joint_group)   # self: envelope, other: all three
print(table.summary())
    table = envelope_group.compare_to(joint_group) # self: envelope, other: all three print(table.summary()) 
    17 subjects paired
          median         total  favour self         p   best
------------------------------------------------------------
R²      0.000272             –       0/17      0.0000  other
AIC      18815.4      496021.5       1/17      0.0007  other
BIC    -156157.7    -2478508.0      17/17      0.0000   self

    Reading the three answers. The cross-validated R² rises with phonemes and words in all 17 subjects, by a median of 2.7·10⁻⁴ on an envelope-alone R² of about 9·10⁻⁴, and the signed-rank test puts that beyond chance. AIC agrees in 16 subjects; BIC prefers the envelope alone in all 17. On EEG neither criterion settles the question: both assume independent samples, and EEG residuals are autocorrelated. In the benchmark's simulations AIC kept a predictor that carried nothing but followed the envelope, in most subjects with ten minutes of data or more, and BIC rejected predictors that did respond (Recommendations). On these recordings, AIC also prefers the envelope beside a placebo — the envelope mixed with the envelope of another part of the story — over the envelope alone, in every subject, while the cross-validated R² falls with it. Phonemes and words earn their place by the measure that can tell.

    16 · What each predictor explains¶

    compare_to says whether the three predictors together beat the envelope. It does not say what each one contributes, and with correlated predictors the kernels cannot say it either: part of what the envelope explains, the onsets could explain in its place. The joint cohort was built with variance_partition=True, so each subject also fitted every subset of the three predictors at the shared λ and on the same folds, and the full model's cross-validated R² splits into regions (Lescroart et al. 2015; de Heer et al. 2017):

    • a predictor's own region is what the model loses without it — section 15's gain, one predictor at a time;
    • a shared region is what several explain alike: how far one can predict in the other's place, not evidence that the response encodes both.

    summary() gives each region's mean over subjects, its share of the full model's R², how many subjects have it positive, and a signed-rank test against zero, corrected over the seven regions.

    plot("venn") draws the regions as circles whose overlaps have the regions' areas, as nearly as three circles allow. A negative region is drawn with the area of its absolute value, hatched, with a dashed outline and a signed label: the full model gains less there than its parts suggest.

    Reading the partition. The full model's cross-validated R² is 1.8·10⁻³ on average. The envelope owns 56 % of it, phonemes 16 % and words 9 %: each explains something the other two cannot, in 16, 17 and 13 of the 17 subjects. About a fifth is shared — 9 % between the envelope and words, 5 % between the envelope and phonemes, 4 % between phonemes and words — and the region all three share, under 1 %, cannot be told from zero. No region came out negative: no predictor costs the full model more than it brings (why one can).

    Words are a subset of phonemes, yet they own 9 % and share only 4 % with them: the response at a word onset is not the response at any other phoneme, as the two kernels of section 13 show. And every shared region says how far one predictor could stand in for another, not that the response encodes both: the 9 % the envelope shares with words is variance either of them predicts, not a response to each.

    17 · One column per phoneme¶

    Phonemes above is one column: an impulse at every phoneme onset, whichever phoneme it is. Di Liberto et al. (2015), whose recordings these are, coded each phoneme by its identity instead: one column per phoneme, 1 while it sounds and 0 otherwise. The feature becomes multivariate, a phoneme × lag kernel per channel, and asks a different question: does the response depend on which phoneme is heard?

    The transcripts name 39 phonemes once their stress marks are dropped (AH0, AH1 and AH2 are one vowel). One, /ʒ/, sounds 5 times in the hour, too few for a kernel, so 38 remain, labelled in IPA as in Di Liberto et al.'s figures. The cohort below fits the envelope beside them, with Part II's window, margin, grid and λ sharing. Its figure is plot_average with two options Part I left at their defaults:

    • channel_reduce="gfp" collapses the channels of the heatmap by their RMS, the global field power, instead of their signed mean. A response that is positive over some electrodes and negative over others, as an auditory one is under a mastoid reference, cancels in the mean and not in the GFP; the GFP loses the sign.
    • cluster_subfeatures=True orders the phonemes by hierarchical clustering of those time courses, the tree on the left, so phonemes that evoke alike sit together.

    from collections import Counter


def phone_intervals(segment: int) -> list[tuple[float, float, str]]:
    """Every phoneme of a run: start and stop in seconds, ARPAbet without stress."""
    text = (TEXTGRIDS / f"audio{segment:02d}.TextGrid").read_text("utf-8")
    block = text.split('name = "phones"')[1].split("item [")[0]
    return [
        (float(start), float(stop), re.sub(r"\d", "", label.strip().upper()))
        for start, stop, label in re.findall(
            r'xmin = ([\d.]+)\s*xmax = ([\d.]+)\s*text = "([^"]*)"', block
        )
        if label.strip().lower() not in SILENCE
    ]


# ARPAbet to IPA, in the order of Di Liberto et al.'s (2015) figure; the last
# four are the transcripts' phonemes that figure does not list.
IPA = {
    "IY": "i", "UW": "u", "AE": "æ", "AA": "ɑ", "EH": "ɛ", "ER": "ɚ", "IH": "ɪ",
    "UH": "ʊ", "AH": "ʌ", "EY": "eɪ", "AY": "aɪ", "OY": "ɔɪ", "AW": "aʊ",
    "Y": "j", "L": "l", "R": "r", "W": "w", "B": "b", "D": "d", "F": "f",
    "HH": "h", "K": "k", "M": "m", "N": "n", "P": "p", "S": "s", "T": "t",
    "V": "v", "Z": "z", "DH": "ð", "NG": "ŋ", "G": "g", "SH": "ʃ", "CH": "tʃ",
    "TH": "θ", "AO": "ɔ", "OW": "oʊ", "JH": "dʒ", "ZH": "ʒ",
}
MIN_OCCURRENCES = 50     # ʒ sounds 5 times in an hour: its kernel would be noise
COUNTS = Counter(p for seg in SEGMENTS for _, _, p in phone_intervals(seg))
PHONEMES = [p for p in IPA if COUNTS[p] >= MIN_OCCURRENCES]


def phoneme_identity(segment: int, n: int) -> np.ndarray:
    """One column per phoneme, 1 while it sounds: Di Liberto et al.'s coding."""
    identity = np.zeros((n, len(PHONEMES)))
    for start, stop, phoneme in phone_intervals(segment):
        if phoneme not in PHONEMES:
            continue
        first, last = round(start * FS), min(round(stop * FS), n)
        identity[first:last, PHONEMES.index(phoneme)] = 1.0
    return identity


def build_identity_subject(subject: int) -> TRFData:
    """One subject's 20 runs with the envelope and the phoneme identities."""
    raws, envelope, identity = [], [], []
    for seg in SEGMENTS:
        raw, predictors = load_aligned_segment(subject, seg)
        raws.append(raw)
        envelope.append(predictors["Envelope"])
        identity.append(phoneme_identity(seg, raw.n_times))
    return TRFData(
        features={"Envelope": envelope, "PhonemeIdentity": identity},
        y=raws, sample_rate=FS, use_gpu=USE_GPU,
    )


print(f"{len(PHONEMES)} phonemes: "
      f"{' '.join(IPA[p] for p in PHONEMES)}")
print(f"left out, fewer than {MIN_OCCURRENCES} times: "
      f"{[IPA[p] for p in IPA if COUNTS[p] < MIN_OCCURRENCES]}")

    from scipy.spatial.distance import pdist
from scipy.stats import spearmanr

VOWELS = {
    "IY", "UW", "AE", "AA", "EH", "ER", "IH", "UH", "AH", "EY", "AY", "OY",
    "AW", "AO", "OW",
}
OBSTRUENTS = {
    "B", "D", "G", "P", "T", "K", "F", "V", "TH", "DH", "S", "Z", "SH", "HH",
    "CH", "JH",
}
first = identity_group.results(identity_group.subject_ids[0])
lags_ms = 1000 * np.asarray(first["delays"]["PhonemeIdentity"]) / FS
kernels = 1e6 * np.stack([      # µV; (subjects, channels, phonemes, lags)
    identity_group.results(sub)["coef_"]["PhonemeIdentity"]
    for sub in identity_group.subject_ids
])
n_subjects = len(kernels)
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)


def gfp(subjects: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """Phoneme x lag GFP of the kernel averaged over ``subjects``."""
    return np.sqrt((kernels[subjects].mean(axis=0) ** 2).mean(axis=0))


def class_peak_ms(heat: np.ndarray, members: set) -> float:
    """Lag of the peak of a class's mean GFP, between 0 and 400 ms."""
    rows = [i for i, p in enumerate(PHONEMES) if p in members]
    inside = (lags_ms >= 0) & (lags_ms <= 400)
    curve = heat[rows][:, inside].mean(axis=0)
    return lags_ms[inside][curve.argmax()]


def obstruent_delay(subjects: np.ndarray) -> float:
    heat = gfp(subjects)
    return class_peak_ms(heat, OBSTRUENTS) - class_peak_ms(heat, VOWELS)


everyone = np.arange(n_subjects)
heat = gfp(everyone)
resampled = [
    obstruent_delay(rng.integers(0, n_subjects, n_subjects))
    for _ in range(1000)
]
low, high = np.percentile(resampled, [2.5, 97.5])
print(
    f"vowels peak at {class_peak_ms(heat, VOWELS):.0f} ms, obstruents at "
    f"{class_peak_ms(heat, OBSTRUENTS):.0f} ms: "
    f"{obstruent_delay(everyone):.0f} ms later, 95 % [{low:.0f}, "
    f"{high:.0f}] over 1000 resamples of the subjects"
)

own_course, tree_distances = [], []
for _ in range(200):
    order = rng.permutation(n_subjects)
    a = gfp(order[:n_subjects // 2])
    b = gfp(order[n_subjects // 2:])
    own_course.append([
        np.corrcoef(a[i], b[i])[0, 1] for i in range(len(PHONEMES))
    ])
    tree_distances.append(spearmanr(
        pdist(a, "correlation"), pdist(b, "correlation")
    )[0])
own_course = np.median(own_course, axis=0)          # one per phoneme
seconds = Counter()
for seg in SEGMENTS:
    for start, stop, phoneme in phone_intervals(seg):
        seconds[phoneme] += stop - start
sounding = np.array([seconds[p] for p in PHONEMES])
print(
    "two random halves of the cohort, 200 times: a phoneme's GFP course "
    f"correlates {np.median(own_course):.2f} with itself, the distances "
    f"behind the tree {np.median(tree_distances):.2f}"
)
print("least repeatable:", ", ".join(
    f"{IPA[PHONEMES[i]]} {own_course[i]:.2f} ({sounding[i]:.0f} s)"
    for i in np.argsort(own_course)[:6]
))
print(
    "repeatability against seconds of sound, rank r = "
    f"{spearmanr(own_course, sounding)[0]:.2f}"
)

start sounding = np.array([seconds[p] for p in PHONEMES]) print( "two random halves of the cohort, 200 times: a phoneme's GFP course " f"correlates {np.median(own_course):.2f} with itself, the distances " f"behind the tree {np.median(tree_distances):.2f}" ) print("least repeatable:", ", ".join( f"{IPA[PHONEMES[i]]} {own_course[i]:.2f} ({sounding[i]:.0f} s)" for i in np.argsort(own_course)[:6] )) print( "repeatability against seconds of sound, rank r = " f"{spearmanr(own_course, sounding)[0]:.2f}" )

    Reading the phonemes. Most rows light up between 60 and 140 ms, and the tree splits them into two large branches. The upper one (red) holds most of the vowels together with /b/, /d/ and /ð/, and peaks between 60 and 100 ms; the lower one (green) holds the fricatives and the voiceless stops, with /l/, /m/ and the short vowels /ɪ/, /ʌ/ and /ʊ/, and peaks between 100 and 140 ms. The cell above checks the one contrast that can be named before looking at the figure: averaged over their rows, the vowels peak at 78 ms and the obstruents (stops, fricatives and affricates) about 30 ms later, and the delay stays positive when the subjects are resampled.

    The tree deserves less trust than its tidy drawing suggests. Split the cohort in two and a phoneme's GFP course correlates about 0.5 with itself in the other half, and the distances the tree is built from about 0.3. The rows that stand alone at the edges, /ŋ/ and /ʃ/ at the top and /dʒ/ and /tʃ/ at the bottom, are among those that do not repeat at all. They are phonemes that sound little: a column is 1 only while its phoneme sounds, and the six least repeatable sound between 10 and 38 seconds in the whole hour. How well a row repeats follows those seconds, and since the GFP is an RMS, a row with no response still draws a faint band, never a dark one. What resampling supports is the delay between vowels and obstruents; which phoneme sits in which branch, and beside which, is this cohort's draw.

    18 · Persisting a fitted cohort¶

    A fitted cohort is a result, and results should outlive the session that produced them. save writes the whole object — kernels, metrics, λ, diagnostics, cached statistics — and trflearn.load restores one with the same API, so every figure above can be redrawn without touching the 4 GB of source data again. The file is left on disk; delete it once you no longer need it.

    19 · Summary¶

    .fif (broadband, ICA-cleaned, mastoid-referenced)
   -> linear-phase FIR 1.5-14 Hz, zero-phase
   -> mne.Raw + Envelope, and Phonemes / Words from the TextGrids
   -> TRFData(y=[Raw, ...])  ->  create_partitions(5 folds, block-stratified)
        |
        |-- Part I   TRFGroup(["Envelope"])                       -> the classic P1/N1/P2 kernel
        |-- Part II  TRFGroup(["Envelope", "Phonemes", "Words"])  -> joint estimation + GVIF
        |            TRFGroup(["Envelope", "PhonemeIdentity"])    -> one kernel per phoneme
        |
   -> grand average -> TFCE over delays x channels -> compare_to -> variance partition

    What was demonstrated. A container of named candidate features from which each model selects its own subset; mne.Raw ingestion carrying the montage all the way through to the group statistics; delay_margin fitting wide and trimming the edge artefact away; λ chosen on R² with Pearson's r and RMSE reported beside it; one λ per cohort by leave-one-subject-out, set against what the mean curve and the median would have picked; design diagnostics before and after other blocks exist to compare against; the complete plotting API at model, cohort and single-subject level; bootstrap distributions per subject; TFCE with a real sensor adjacency; whether phonemes and words earn their place, by the cross-validated R² and by AIC/BIC; what each predictor explains alone and what they explain alike; a multivariate feature, one column per phoneme, drawn as a GFP heatmap ordered by clustering its rows, with a split-half check of that order; and a save/load round trip.

    What was not established. Held-out correlations of a few hundredths are normal for single-trial continuous speech, but they are small. Nothing here says the envelope is the right representation of speech — only that it predicts above chance. Section 15 ranks two specifications against each other; it does not suggest the winner is correct, and section 16's shared regions say that predictors can stand in for each other, not that the response encodes each. Section 17's tree orders 38 kernels each estimated from seconds to minutes of sound: what survives resampling the cohort is the delay between vowels and obstruents, not the order of the leaves. And every result inherits the upstream choices described in section 1, including a band-pass that shapes the width of every kernel plotted above.
